notes: Part II LTA 1954 break-clause appeal; fresh post-trial evidence and varied break date are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Davy's v City of London: redevelopment break clause and fresh evidence on appeal
key_facts: Davy's wine bar at 120 Fenchurch Street sought a new 14-year business tenancy under section 26 of the 1954 Act after the City Corporation served no counter-notice.
The county court judge ordered a rolling redevelopment break clause exercisable after five years on eleven months' notice, with rent agreed at £50,000.
After trial the building was sold to Saxon Land rather than Coronation Land's island-site developer, and fresh evidence was admitted on appeal.
Lewison J held the judge was not wrong on the original evidence but varied the break clause to operate from June 2008 after belated compliance and Saxon Land's fallback sale strategy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Mayor's and City of London County Court on the terms of a break clause in an unopposed new tenancy under Part II of the 1954 Act, with post-trial fresh evidence.
enrichment.outcome: The landlord's appeal was allowed in part; the break clause was varied to eleven months' notice not to be served before 1 July 2007, expiring on or after 1 June 2008.
enrichment.ratio: On a Part II new-tenancy appeal where fresh post-trial evidence is admitted, the court must take that evidence into account and may treat the judge's discretionary break-clause order as wrong if later events show a fixed term would impede the landlord's realistic redevelopment or sale strategy, while still balancing tenant security against redevelopment.
legal_issues: Whether the county court judge applied the correct legal test for inserting a redevelopment break clause under section 35
Whether post-trial fresh evidence could be deployed on appeal and whether the appeal was a review or rehearing
What break-clause terms were reasonable after Saxon Land acquired the property and pursued a different redevelopment strategy
The relevant date for determining the terms of the new tenancy where section 64 continues the current tenancy pending appeal
linked_authorities: JH Edwards & Sons Ltd v Central London Commercial Estates Ltd [1984] 2 EGLR 103
Amalgamated Investment & Property Co Ltd v Texas Commerce International Bank Ltd [1982] QB 84
Asiansky Television Ltd v Bayer-Rosin [2001] EWCA Civ 1792

confidence.notes: Detailed first-instance and appellate reasoning on break-clause discretion and use of fresh evidence is explicit.

notes: Right-to-buy JR case management; late council participation permitted on terms.

enrichment.short_title: Terry v Tower Hamlets: late permission to defend right-to-buy judicial review
key_facts: Mr Terry, an 86-year-old council tenant in poor health, brought judicial review over his right-to-buy discount after Tower Hamlets failed to file an acknowledgment of service.
The council applied at the substantive hearing for permission to defend, acknowledging that without permission the claim would succeed and the tenant would obtain a substantial discount windfall.
The dispute turned on whether a letter posted by the tenant was received by the council, affecting the discount calculation.

Munby J permitted the council to defend on terms debarring reliance on section 181(3) for costs incurred after Charles J's permission order, and transferred the case urgently to the Queen's Bench Division.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in judicial review for permission for a defaulting local authority to participate and defend a right-to-buy claim.
enrichment.outcome: The council was given permission to defend subject to a costs condition on section 181(3); the claim was transferred to the Queen's Bench Division for urgent trial and the council was ordered to pay for a transcript of the ruling.
enrichment.ratio: Where a public authority has seriously defaulted in judicial review but denying it any opportunity to defend would likely confer a windfall on the claimant while the real issue is factual, the court may permit late participation on appropriate terms so long as the claimant can be compensated in costs and procedural fairness is preserved.
legal_issues: Whether Tower Hamlets should be permitted to defend after failing to acknowledge service
Whether the claim was essentially private landlord-and-tenant law rather than public law
The effect of section 181(3) where proceedings were brought in the High Court instead of the county court
What case-management directions were needed for an urgent factual trial

confidence.notes: Interlocutory case-management ruling is clear though the substantive right-to-buy merits were not decided.

notes: Drink-drive case stated; section 7(7) warning point clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Beatrice: section 7(7) drink-drive warning must be given by constable
key_facts: Christopher Beatrice was convicted by magistrates of driving with excess alcohol after a hospital blood sample taken following a road accident.
PC Cresswell said he worked through the drink-drive hospital procedure booklet, but the justices emphasised a warning given by the police surgeon Dr Howlett rather than by the constable.
The prosecution accepted that a doctor's warning alone cannot satisfy section 7(7), though undisputed evidence suggested the standard booklet procedure may have been followed.
The Divisional Court quashed the conviction because there was a real possibility the bench had been misdirected that the doctor's warning sufficed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from South East Surrey Justices after the court directed a case on drink-drive procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed on question iii; no order for a rehearing; appellant awarded costs out of central funds before legal aid and legal aid assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 7(7) of the Road Traffic Act 1988 the statutory warning before requiring a specimen must be given by a constable, not a doctor; where justices may have relied on a doctor's warning alone the conviction cannot stand even if other evidence might have supported an inference that the officer gave the warning.
legal_issues: Whether the appellant had been given the section 7(7) warning of prosecution
Whether a warning by the police surgeon could satisfy the statutory requirement
Whether the justices could infer from the hospital procedure booklet that PC Cresswell gave the warning
Whether the court should order a rehearing after quashing the conviction
linked_authorities: Murray v Director of Public Prosecutions [1993] RTR 209

confidence.notes: The legal error and quashing order on the sole live question are clearly stated.

notes: Attorney General reference; unduly lenient s18 sentence but no increase imposed.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 77/2004: unduly lenient s18 head-kick sentence not increased
key_facts: A 19-year-old offender pleaded guilty at a late stage to section 18 GBH with intent after kicking a defenceless victim in the head during a pub affray, causing jaw fractures requiring metal plates.
He was sentenced to a two-year community rehabilitation order with Think First, a six-month curfew, and £1,000 compensation.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient, citing the kick to the head, shod foot, and prior violence conviction.

The Court of Appeal held an expected sentence of about three years' detention was appropriate but declined to increase the sentence because double jeopardy and the offender's partial compliance made further custody contrary to the public interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 for an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; sentence held unduly lenient but the court exercised its discretion not to interfere and increase custody.
enrichment.ratio: A late guilty plea to section 18 GBH with intent involving a deliberate kick to the head of a prone victim would normally attract about three years in a young offender institution, but on an Attorney General's reference the court may still refrain from increasing a non-custodial sentence where double jeopardy, partial sentence completion, and loss of employment/compensation capacity make a short further term pointless.
legal_issues: Whether a community sentence was unduly lenient for section 18 GBH with intent
The weight of aggravating features including kicking a defenceless victim in the head
Whether the Court of Appeal should increase the sentence despite double jeopardy and partial compliance with the original order

confidence.notes: Finding of undue lenience and discretionary decision not to increase are both explicit.

notes: Section 69 salvage arbitration appeal; tug/tow fault apportionment under Article 18.

enrichment.short_title: Maridive tugs v Key Singapore: Article 18 salvage fault apportionment appeal
key_facts: Maridive tugs rendered salvage services to the jack-up rig Key Singapore in severe weather in the Eastern Mediterranean after tow wires parted.
The original arbitrator awarded US$1.8 million salvage, reducing a US$3 million base award for the tugs' contributory fault; the appeal arbitrator reduced the award to US$1 million.
Both arbitrators found fault in failing to heave to, but differed on whether tug masters and the rig were equally to blame.
David Steel J dismissed the section 69 appeal, holding that overall command of the tow does not as a matter of law make the tow more blameworthy when both parties failed to heave to.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 69 appeal with permission against an appeal arbitrator's award varying salvage remuneration and fault apportionment under Article 18 of the Salvage Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the appeal arbitrator was entitled to treat tug and rig as equally at fault for failing to heave to.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 18 of the Salvage Convention relative fault must be assessed by causative potency and blameworthiness; nineteenth-century authorities on tug obedience to tow do not establish that the party in overall command is necessarily more at fault when both tug and tow fail to take the same precaution.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal arbitrator erred in apportioning equal blame for failure to heave to
Whether established tug-and-tow law required greater fault to be attributed to the rig as overall controller
The correct approach to Article 18 partial deprivation of salvage payment for contributory fault
linked_authorities: The Duke of Manchester (1846) 2 W Rob 470
The Minnie Sommers v The Francis Batey (1921) 8 Ll L Rep 247

confidence.notes: Central question of law and dismissal are clearly reasoned, though salvage quantum details are secondary.

notes: Patent fiduciary breach application to amend; knowing receipt and derivative action issues.

enrichment.short_title: Fraser v Oystertec: late amendment for knowing receipt of misappropriated patents
key_facts: Patents including the Oystertec Converter were purportedly transferred by directors Davidson and Binney to Davidson and then sold to Oystertec ahead of its 2001 flotation.
Easyrad obtained summary judgment that the Oystertec Converter transfer was unauthorised but was denied a declaration of ownership because of laches; equitable compensation was awarded instead.
The claimants sought belatedly to join the solicitor Warburton and amend to plead knowing receipt and imputed notice against Oystertec.

Lightman J refused joinder of Warburton to preserve the trial date, allowed notice-imputation amendments conditionally on £35,000 paid in, and deferred Easyrad's knowing-receipt amendment pending derivative-action permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to amend and join an additional defendant in ongoing Chancery proceedings concerning misappropriated patents and breach of fiduciary duty.
enrichment.outcome: Late joinder of the solicitor refused; paragraph 7 notice amendments allowed; knowing-receipt amendments against Oystertec allowed subject to £35,000 security; Easyrad amendments deferred pending derivative-action approval.
enrichment.ratio: Very late amendments may be permitted where they raise triable issues without vacating an imminent trial and prejudice can be compensated by costs or a payment into court; a knowing-receipt claim cannot be pursued by Easyrad in respect of the Oystertec Converter where summary judgment already proceeded on the basis title never passed, and derivative authority is required before expanding a derivative claim.
legal_issues: Whether the solicitor should be joined for dishonest assistance at a late stage
Whether Oystertec could be liable for knowing receipt and constructive trust with imputed notice through directors and solicitor
Whether Easyrad could add a knowing-receipt claim after electing for equitable compensation on a no-title-passed basis
Whether continued derivative proceedings remained appropriate after change in control of Easyrad
linked_authorities: Cobbold v London Borough of Greenwich [1999] CA

confidence.notes: Interlocutory rulings are detailed though several merits issues were expressly left to trial.

notes: Letters-of-intent 'if' contract trial; £10m cap and quantum meruit rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Mowlem v Stena: £10 million cap in final letter-of-intent contract
key_facts: Mowlem carried out marine and onshore works at Holyhead Terminal 5 for Stena under a series of letters of intent treated as superseding 'if' contracts.
The final letter dated 4 July 2003 authorised work subject to payment of substantiated costs up to £10 million and referred to proceeding until 18 July 2003.
Mowlem continued work after that date and above the cap, arguing implied terms, further contract, waiver, estoppel, or quantum meruit.
The TCC held the 4 July letter governed all work, the £10 million cap applied regardless of date or instructions, and no quantum meruit arose while the contract subsisted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court for declarations on entitlement to payment for works under letters of intent.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; counterclaim succeeded with declaration that Mowlem's entitlement to payment was subject to a maximum of £10 million.
enrichment.ratio: Where a final letter of intent creates an 'if' contract superseding earlier letters, Stena's obligation to pay substantiated costs is capped at the stated maximum for all authorised work until rescission or formal contract execution; the date in the letter is an estimate of programme coverage not a temporal limit on the cap, and quantum meruit cannot arise while a valid contract governs the work.
legal_issues: Whether work after 18 July 2003 or above £10 million was payable outside the final letter of intent
Whether an implied term, waiver, estoppel, or new contract arose from Stena's insistence on completion
Whether the £10 million figure was a cap on all work or only work until a particular date
Whether Mowlem could claim quantum meruit while the 'if' contract remained in force
linked_authorities: British Steel Corporation v Cleveland Bridge & Engineering Co Ltd (1983) BLR 94
Gilbert & Partners v Knight [1968] 2 All ER 248

confidence.notes: Final declarations and contractual construction are clearly decided on agreed facts.

notes: Solicitors Act s70(3) special circumstances application dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Lakhani v Eversheds: special circumstances for late bill assessment refused
key_facts: Mr Lakhani instructed Eversheds on employment and compromise-agreement negotiations with Tilda Ltd after periods of mental ill-health.
He paid ten bills totalling about £29,432 delivered between May 2003 and February 2004, applying for detailed assessment on the last possible day under section 70(3).
He alleged inadequate costs estimates, lack of cost-benefit advice, and duplication between fee earners in breach of the Solicitors Costs Information and Client Care Code.
The costs judge found he had received regular bills, oral estimates, and cost-benefit advice and dismissed the Part 8 claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for detailed assessment of solicitors' bills outside the one-month period, relying on special circumstances under section 70(3).
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no order for detailed assessment of the challenged bills.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to give further written estimates after an initial client-care letter does not necessarily amount to special circumstances justifying late assessment where the client received monthly bills, frequent oral cost and cost-benefit advice, and understood the mounting costs; isolated duplication attributable to the client's choice to contact both fee earners is insufficient without a Code breach.
legal_issues: Whether special circumstances existed under section 70(3) for assessing bills delivered and paid more than one month before the application
Whether Eversheds breached the Costs Information and Client Care Code on estimates and cost-benefit advice
Whether duplication between partner and assistant fee earners warranted assessment

confidence.notes: Findings on each special-circumstance head and dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Eritrean asylum appeal dismissed; no persecution risk for minor son of dissident.

enrichment.short_title: Fesum v SSHD: Eritrean minor son of dissident not at risk
key_facts: Aynom Fesum, an Eritrean national aged 16 on arrival, claimed asylum because his dissident army-officer father had been arrested and police had assaulted him and his mother at home.
The adjudicator accepted the family incident but found no evidence that non-political relatives of government opponents were persecuted.

The Immigration Appeal Tribunal reviewed general country evidence on G-15 dissidents and concluded the appellant, as a minor child of a supporter rather than a prominent dissident, was not at real risk.
The Court of Appeal held the tribunal's reasons were adequate and noted he could make a fresh claim now he was 18 and potentially liable for conscription.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissing an asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where country evidence shows risk to dissidents and their associates but not to non-political family members generally, a specialist tribunal may properly conclude that a minor child of a lesser supporter is not at real risk of persecution on return, provided its reasons explain why the claimant falls outside the at-risk class.
legal_issues: Whether the minor son of an arrested dissident army officer faced a real risk of persecution in Eritrea
Whether the IAT gave adequate reasons for rejecting the asylum claim
The relevance of general country evidence on the G-15 group and relatives of dissidents

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on adequacy of reasons is clear though fact-sensitive country conditions underlie the outcome.

notes: Search-and-seizure contempt application; Mr Hogan fined, Mrs Hogan not imprisoned.

enrichment.short_title: Heidelberg v Hogan: contempt of search-and-seizure order over pirated software
key_facts: Heidelberg claimed its confidential printing-press CD-ROMs were being sold on eBay, traced to Mrs Julie Hogan and her sister Charlene Parkinson.
Park J made a search-and-seizure and freezing order against Mrs Hogan; on 15 July 2004 the supervising solicitor attempted execution at the Hogans' home.
Mrs Hogan refused entry, made prohibited telephone calls, and followed her husband's instructions; Mr Hogan removed computer equipment over the fence and obstructed the search.
Mann J found serious contempt against both but imposed no prison sentence on Mrs Hogan and fined Mr Hogan £5,000 after belated compliance and bankruptcy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Committal application for contempt of court for breach of search-and-seizure and asset-freezing orders.
enrichment.outcome: Contempt established against both defendants on core heads; Mrs Hogan received no further sanction; Mr Hogan fined £5,000 and avoided imprisonment by belated purge of contempt.
enrichment.ratio: Those in control of premises and anyone who knowingly assists breach of a search-and-seizure order must comply without question; removing listed items and directing another person to refuse entry constitute serious contempt even if the order was explained rather than formally served, though belated restoration of property and cooperation may justify a fine rather than immediate imprisonment.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Hogan was in contempt for refusing entry, making telephone calls, and failing to give immediate disclosure
Whether Mr Hogan was liable for obstructing the search, instructing his wife, and removing listed items
Whether coercion or Human Rights Act Articles 8 and 10 provided a defence to the telephone-call restrictions
What sentence was appropriate where contempt was established but later purged

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on each contempt head and sentencing outcome are explicit.
